ext.code.replace.deployment: Not provided by this deployment ({name}). Ask your admin to check the router stack's settings, then reload this page.
ext.code.replace.host: The remote machine you connect to with SSH.
ext.code.replace.home: Your home folder written out in full, such as /Users/alice, /home/alice or C:\Users\alice. Claude Desktop expands neither ~ nor %USERPROFILE%.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.where: In Claude Desktop, turn on Help → Troubleshooting → Enable Developer Mode, then open Developer → Configure Third-Party Inference…. Save this block as a .json file and load it with Import configuration… in the configuration picker at the top right (or enter the same values in the form), then click Apply Changes and relaunch.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.token: The credential helper runs llmar credential. It prints the token and an x-api-key header with the same token: Claude Desktop sends the token as a bearer token, which the gateway checks, and adds the header, which the router identifies you by. With the TTL at 4 minutes, Claude Desktop checks the credential before each turn; llmar answers from its cache and refreshes the token before it expires. No API key is needed.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.models: Claude Desktop accepts only model ids that look like Claude, so the router serves these four aliases: claude-auto (the router picks the tier), claude-opus-auto (frontier), claude-sonnet-auto (standard) and claude-haiku-auto (fast). The gateway's model list is empty, so they are listed here and Claude Desktop skips model discovery. behavesAs gives each alias the effort levels and context window of a Claude model (Claude Desktop 4.29.0 or later), and anthropicFamilyTier sends Claude Desktop's opus, sonnet and haiku requests, from sub-agents for example, to the matching tier.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.aliases: This deployment's routing policy lacks the aliases Claude Desktop needs ({aliases}). Ask your admin to add them.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.aliasesAdmi: This deployment's routing policy lacks the aliases Claude Desktop needs ({aliases}). Add them under Routing policy → Aliases, then reload this page.
ext.getStarted.claudeDesktop.update: llmar credential is new: if llmar answers "invalid choice: 'credential'", install llmar again (the first step).
ext.getStarted.platform.label: Operating system
ext.getStarted.windows.step1: Run this in PowerShell on Windows itself. Inside WSL, follow the macOS / Linux / WSL steps instead. llmar needs Python 3.9 or later: python --version must print a version. Windows does not run a script by its first line, so three .cmd files in %USERPROFILE%\bin run it as llmar, llmar-token and llmar-login.
ext.getStarted.windows.configure: This saves the deployment's values in %USERPROFILE%\.config\llmar\config.json: sign-in domain, client id, scope, callback ports and gateway URL. The file holds no secrets. The block goes in on standard input, because PowerShell changes the quotes of a JSON argument.
ext.getStarted.windows.signIn: llmar login opens your browser at the sign-in page. Sign in with your password. llmar then saves a refresh token in %USERPROFILE%\.config\llmar\. The folder is inside your user profile, which Windows keeps to your account by default; llmar does not check Windows permissions itself.
ext.getStarted.windows.claudeCode.where: In %USERPROFILE%\.claude\settings.json, or a project's .claude\settings.json. On Windows, Claude Code runs apiKeyHelper through cmd, which fills in %USERPROFILE%. Keep the inner quotes: they hold a profile folder with spaces together.
ext.getStarted.windows.codex.auth: Required: Codex does not fill in %USERPROFILE% (or any variable) in config.toml, so the two paths above do not work as saved. After saving the configuration, run this command once: it replaces %USERPROFILE% in both paths with your profile folder. Until then Codex finds neither the model catalog nor llmar-token.cmd. Codex runs llmar-token.cmd for the Authorization header and refreshes it every 4 minutes. The single quotes around the paths are TOML literal strings, which keep the backslashes as they are.
ext.getStarted.faq.title: FAQ
ext.getStarted.faq.configure.q: llmar configure says “~/.config is writable by others without the sticky bit”
ext.getStarted.faq.configure.a: Ubuntu's default umask makes ~/.config group-writable. Current llmar accepts that when the group is your own private group. With an older copy, run this (or set LLMAR_CONFIG_DIR, and set it for Claude Code and Codex too):
ext.getStarted.faq.redirectPort.q: What goes in redirect_port in the Codex config?
ext.getStarted.faq.redirectPort.a: This page fills it in: it is the loopback port Codex listens on for its own sign-in ({port}), registered for this deployment. Keep it as shown.
ext.getStarted.faq.gatewaySignIn.q: Codex: “Gateway sign-in required or unavailable” after signing in
ext.getStarted.faq.gatewaySignIn.a: Codex could not store its sign-in: Linux without a keyring (servers, SSH sessions). Uncomment this line in the gateway_oauth table, start Codex and sign in again. The sign-in then lives in $CODEX_HOME/secrets/gateway_oauth.json (mode 0600).
ext.getStarted.faq.ssh.q: Signing in on a remote machine over SSH
ext.getStarted.faq.ssh.a: Both sign-ins return to 127.0.0.1 on the machine that runs the tool. Forward the callback ports when you connect, then open the printed sign-in URL on your own computer (llmar login --no-browser prints it).
ext.getStarted.faq.path.q: Why does the Codex auth command need an absolute path?
ext.getStarted.faq.path.a: Codex does not expand ~ in the auth command. After saving the configuration, run this to replace it with your home directory:
ext.getStarted.faq.pathWindows.q: Why does the Codex auth command need an absolute path?
ext.getStarted.faq.pathWindows.a: Codex does not fill in %USERPROFILE% or ~ in the auth command. After saving the configuration, run this to replace %USERPROFILE% with your profile folder:
ext.getStarted.faq.winPython.q: “python is not recognized”, or the Microsoft Store opens
ext.getStarted.faq.winPython.a: Python is not installed, or it is not on your PATH. Install Python 3.9 or later from python.org or the Microsoft Store, then open a new PowerShell window. If only the py launcher works on your machine, replace python with py -3 in the three .cmd files in %USERPROFILE%\bin.
ext.getStarted.faq.status2.a: llmar has no valid sign-in. Run llmar-token in a terminal to see why; usually you run llmar login again (every {refreshDays} days, or after an admin disabled and re-enabled you).
ext.getStarted.faq.maxTokens.a: That works. GPT models on Bedrock reject max_tokens, so the router renames it to max_completion_tokens when a GPT model serves the request. Other models get the request unchanged.
ext.getStarted.faq.whichModel.a: Every response carries x-router-model (the model that served it) and x-router-decision. The Decisions page lists each request with its basis.
ext.getStarted.faq.metadata.q: Codex warns “Model metadata for 'auto' not found”
ext.getStarted.faq.metadata.a: Codex is not reading the model catalog, so it caps auto at 272K (sessions compact at about 258K). Create ~/.codex/llmar-models.json with the command on the Codex tab and check the model_catalog_json path in config.toml.
ext.getStarted.faq.codexPin.q: Codex: a 400 pin-not-allowed on the Decisions page while the session works
ext.getStarted.faq.codexPin.a: Some Codex background passes name a model of their own instead of auto, such as memory extraction at startup (gpt-6-luna). The router refuses a name that is neither an alias nor an allowed model, so only that pass fails; your conversation is not affected. Keep this table in config.toml (it is in the snippet above), or set generate_memories = false there to turn memories off. An admin can instead add the name as an alias on the Routing policy page.
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeBedrock.q: Claude Code shows “Amazon Bedrock” in its header, or “The provided model identifier is invalid”
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeBedrock.a: Claude Code is calling Bedrock directly: CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK is set in your environment or in another settings file, and it wins over ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Keep "CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK": "0" in the router settings (it is in the snippet above), restart Claude Code and check that the header no longer says Amazon Bedrock. To see what is set:
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeApiKey.q: Claude Code warns “Both apiKeyHelper and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set”, or my requests show as unattributed
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeApiKey.a: Claude Code still signs in to the gateway with your llmar token, but it sends the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY value in x-api-key, the header the router reads your identity from (an x-api-key in ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS does the same). Requests work but count as unattributed: your tier limit and budget do not apply to them, and they get 401 once your admin sets identity to Require. Unset it for router sessions and remove it from your settings files:
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeModel.q: Claude Code: “Model "auto" isn't recognized · context assumed to be 200k tokens”
ext.getStarted.faq.claudeModel.a: Claude Code does not know the router's alias auto, so it assumes a 200K context window and compacts the conversation at 200K. The router's Claude models have a 1M window. Keep this line in the env block of the router settings (it is in the snippet above) and restart Claude Code. Use a smaller value only if your admin limits you to a model with a smaller window.
ext.getStarted.faq.expired403.q: Claude Code: “Please run /login · API Error: 403 insufficient_scope” in the middle of a session
ext.getStarted.faq.expired403.a: Not a permission problem and not an Anthropic sign-in: the gateway answers an expired access token with 403 insufficient_scope. Don't run /login; send the prompt again. llmar hands out a new token when the same token is asked for again right away. If it keeps happening, run this to see whether llmar needs you to sign in again, and check that your clock is right (date -u):
ext.familyRules.title: Suggested fast rules (from traffic)
ext.familyRules.pagination.label: Suggested fast rules pages
ext.familyRules.description: Requests that share a template (the same tools and system prompt) form a template family. A family whose turns look simple can go to the fast tier through a policy rule, which decides before the assessor.
ext.familyRules.proxy.header: The evidence is a proxy, not a quality label ({version})
ext.familyRules.proxy.body: A consulted turn counts as fast when the assessor's task facts say: no code edits, no earlier failures, and lookup or routine depth. Its tier opinion is not used. The proxy is weak for a single turn; a family qualifies only when the lower bound over many turns is high. Read the sample decisions before you approve, and watch the family's health after activation.
ext.familyRules.summary: {families, plural, =0 {No template families} one {# template family} other {# template families}} in {from} – {to}: {requests} requests, {turns} turns with assessor facts.
ext.familyRules.empty: No template-family data yet. It starts with the usage-ingest version that records families, and needs the assessor to run (observe or auto).
ext.familyRules.health: {errors} errors · {failovers} failovers · {hints} hints · user turns fast {fast} / standard {standard} / frontier {frontier}
ext.familyRules.unknownFacts: {count} turns with incomplete facts are not counted.
ext.familyRules.activeNote: Active: the rule decides these turns, so the assessor is no longer consulted and the evidence stops growing. Watch errors, failovers and turns served above fast.
ext.familyRules.approved: Added {id} to this edit. Save the draft, validate and activate to put it in force.
ext.familyRules.revoked: Removed the rule for {family} from this edit. Activate to put the change in force.
ext.policy.rule.edit.help.permissionMode: Comma-separated modes as the client reports them: plan or auto. Other modes (default, acceptEdits, bypassPermissions, dontAsk) send nothing, so no rule can match them.
ext.policy.rule.edit.help.effort: Comma-separated levels as the client sends them: low, medium, high, xhigh or max. Claude Code sends one on every request, high by default, so only the others tell you something; Codex sends one only when the user sets it.
ext.policy.rule.edit.error.token: Each value starts with a lowercase letter, then letters or hyphens (at most 32 characters).
ext.familyRules.minTurns: With a lower bound of {minLb} a family needs at least {turns, number} turns, all of them proxy fast (the minimum n is {minN, number}).
ext.familyRules.guide.why.title: In one sentence
ext.familyRules.guide.why.body:
Some requests look the same every time and are always easy work. The console finds them and suggests a fixed rule: send them straight to the cheaper, faster model instead of asking every time how hard the task is.
Normally every request first goes to the assessor (a small model) to judge difficulty before a tier is picked, and that step costs time and money. A CI script that runs hundreds of times a day to look things up or tidy formatting does not need that check each time.
ext.familyRules.guide.family.title: What a template family is
ext.familyRules.guide.family.body: Think of it as the same kind of request. Every request carries a list of tools and an opening instruction (the system prompt). Requests where both are identical belong to one family, like different forms filled in from the same template. Requests from the same tool, the same script or the same way of working usually land in the same family.
ext.familyRules.guide.judge.title: How the console decides a family is simple
ext.familyRules.guide.judge.body:
Each time the assessor looks at a request, the console notes three things: does it edit code, did anything fail before, and how deep does it need to think (a quick lookup or routine work, or real reasoning)? No code edits, no earlier failures and simple depth means that turn counts as simple.
One judgement is not reliable, so the console looks at many. A family becomes a Candidate only when it has enough turns in the window (14 days by default), nearly all of them simple, and the result holds up statistically rather than by luck. With the default settings that takes roughly seventy-plus turns that are all simple.
ext.familyRules.guide.steps.title: What you do
ext.familyRules.guide.steps.body:
Find families with the status Candidate in the table below.
Open the links under Sample decisions and check what those requests actually do: make sure they really are easy work.
Click Add rule. The rule only goes into the configuration you are editing; it is not in force yet.
Save the draft, validate and activate as with any policy change. The rule takes effect only after activation.
After activation, watch the Health column: errors and frequent model switches. If something looks wrong, click Remove rule and activate again to undo it.
ext.familyRules.guide.notes.title: Good to know
ext.familyRules.guide.notes.body:
The rule decides: once active, the family goes straight to the fast tier without asking the assessor, so no new difficulty records build up. From then on, judge the rule by its health numbers.
An update can retire the rule: when the client is upgraded or its tools or system prompt change, the requests become a new family, the old rule stops matching, and the new family has to build up evidence and be added again.
Chats with people rarely qualify: what people ask varies too much to pass the thresholds. This is mainly for automated scripts, CI and other fixed workflows.
Some moments never switch models: while the model is in the middle of a tool loop it keeps its model; a rule applies only when a new user turn starts.

ext.adminRules.title: Admin rules
ext.adminRules.description: Your own rules for the assessor, judged in the same call as the pack's rules. A new rule only records whether it matched (observe); turn it on (act) when its evidence looks right. A match never raises the tier of a sub-agent.
ext.adminRules.empty: No admin rules. Add one here, or describe one in a sentence on the Routing policy page.
ext.adminRules.presetsHint: Preset: animation, video or visually designed UI work → Hard (frontier), in observe state.
ext.adminRules.cost: Each rule adds about 100–150 cached prompt tokens and 30–50 output tokens to every consultation.
ext.adminRules.col.followUps: Later turns served below its tier
ext.adminRules.modal.title: Admin rule
ext.adminRules.field.instruction.help: The assessor sees only a task card: the latest and the first user message, the agent's last reply, tool names and counts. Describe the task, not the model. To cover follow-up turns, add “Judge the session's task, the first user message included.”
ext.adminRules.field.id.help: x- followed by lowercase letters, digits or hyphens. Editing a rule's text or tier starts its evidence afresh.
ext.adminRules.error.id: x- followed by 1–38 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens.
ext.adminRules.error.idTaken: Another admin rule has this id.
ext.adminRules.warning.off: The assessor is off: admin rules are kept but not judged.
ext.adminRules.warning.observe: The assessor only records (observe): admin rules are judged and recorded, but even rules in act state do not change tiers.
ext.adminRules.warning.routerObserve: Routing mode is Observe only: models never change, so rules in act state only change what the savings pages say Auto would do.
ext.adminRules.evidence.title: Admin rule evidence
ext.adminRules.evidence.description: Counted over fresh assessor consultations (retries and reused answers are not counted). Evidence is kept per rule text: editing a rule's text or tier starts it afresh.
ext.adminRules.evidence.empty: No admin rules and no evidence yet. Evidence starts with the usage-ingest version that records admin rules, and needs the assessor to run (observe or auto).
ext.adminRules.status.oldUnknown: Earlier text (not found in recent versions)
ext.adminRules.missing: {count, plural, one {# time} other {# times}} not judged by the model
ext.adminRules.matchedSub: {count, plural, one {# match} other {# matches}} on sub-agents (tier not raised)
ext.adminRules.effect.observe: If on, would change: fast {fast} · standard {standard} · frontier {frontier}
ext.adminRules.effect.act: Acted on {count, plural, one {# turn} other {# turns}}
ext.adminRules.followUps.observe: Counted only for rules in act state.
ext.adminRules.followUps.warning: The assessor or the router is not in auto mode: later turns are served at the default tier and count as below the rule's tier.
ext.adminRules.turnedOn: Turned {id} on in this edit. Activate to put it in force.
